name: Deviancy amplification spiral
statement: A hard reaction to a small deviation is held to enlarge it, because coverage and policing make the deviants more visible and more separate, which brings a harder reaction again.
meaning: The model is a feedback loop with four steps. A minor deviation is noticed and treated as worth punishing. The people involved are separated from ordinary society and come to see themselves as the thing they have been called. They group with others in the same position and behave more like the label, which draws heavier control, and the loop turns again. The media supply the step that makes the loop public, because most people learn about deviance from reports rather than from contact. Cohen's addition was to name the audience side of it. A moral panic is a period in which a group is defined as a threat to society's values, presented by the press in a stylised way, and denounced by editors, bishops, politicians and accredited experts. The claim is about the reaction, not about the original behaviour. It says the response to a problem is part of what the problem becomes.

origin.where: Social Deviance: Social Policy, Action and Research, Tavistock, 311 pages
origin.note: Wilkins set out the feedback sequence in chapter 4 and called it deviation amplification. That book was not read here, so his wording reaches this page through Stanley Cohen's account of it, which describes the language as mechanistic and derived from cybernetic theory. The idea travels now under Cohen's name because of Folk Devils and Moral Panics, first published in 1972 by MacGibbon and Kee, which applied the model to the mods and rockers. The credit for the phrase moral panic sits in the first note to Cohen's introduction to the third edition, read here as a separate scan. He says the term was first used by Jock Young, in a 1971 chapter of Cohen's own edited collection Images of Deviance, at page 37, and that both men probably picked it up from Marshall McLuhan's Understanding Media, published in 1964.

evidence: Cohen's fieldwork ran from 1964 to 1967. His research period covered the three-year cycle of bank holidays from Easter 1964 to September 1966. He gathered national and local press, tape recordings of most BBC news broadcasts over the holiday weekends, Hansard, council papers, court reports and his own observation at the resorts. One agency cutting file on Margate over Whitsun 1964 held 724 items dated between 15 May and 12 June. Of those, 223 were editorials or columnist comments and 121 were letters. The first event was at Clacton over Easter 1964, when Easter Sunday was the coldest for eighty years. Windows were broken, some beach huts were wrecked, and one boy fired a starting pistol in the air. Ninety-seven people were arrested and twenty-four were charged, of whom twenty-three had previous convictions. About a tenth of the Clacton offenders was charged with an offence involving violence. Four were charged with what Cohen calls non-hooligan offences, among them stealing half a pint of petrol and obtaining an ice cream by fraud. His table of local authority estimates puts the damage at £513 in Clacton, £100 in Bournemouth, £400 in Brighton and £250 in Margate. Police overtime at Brighton over Whitsun 1964 came to £2,000, four times the Clacton damage bill. The next four bank holidays cost Brighton £17,000 in overtime, of which £13,000 was above what it normally spent. Cohen's evidence for the amplification step is observation and interview rather than measurement. He describes police reading hairstyle and dress as signs of trouble, magistrates using their powers to make examples, and crowds hardening against the police as the enemy shifted from rival group to force.

examples.text: A handful of pupils wear an unusual coat, the school writes a rule against it and names them in assembly. The coat becomes a badge, more pupils take it up to be counted among them, and the school answers with detentions. Each turn of that loop was set off by the last response.

examples.tag: The skaters and the local paper
examples.text: Complaints about noise at a car park bring officers and a report calling the skaters a gang. Being handled as one draws the loose group together, new arrivals come for the name, and the next round of complaints is about something larger than the first.

Moderators ban a few argumentative posters, who set up a board of their own where the arguing is the point. The sharper version that grows there is then cited as proof the ban was needed. What the reaction produced is being read as what it found.

replication.headline: No attempt to repeat Cohen's analysis or to measure a full amplification loop was found, the quantitative work that exists tests one link at a time, and the pooled trial evidence is not significant on the measure most often quoted from it.
replication.detail: Crossref searches on 21 September 2026 for replications of Cohen or of Wilkins returned dictionary entries, commentary and later case studies rather than repeat tests. The reference lists of the papers read here point the same way. Two links have been measured separately. On the first, running from coverage to public alarm, Lowry, Nio and Leitner tracked network television crime reporting, survey answers and FBI crime rates from 1978 to 1998. The share of Americans naming crime as the most important problem facing the country rose from 5% in March 1992 to 52% in August 1994. Their television news variables alone accounted for almost four times more variance in that share than actual crime rates did. On the second, running from official reaction to further deviance, Petrosino, Turpin-Petrosino and Guckenburg pooled 29 controlled trials covering 7,304 juveniles, reported between 1973 and 2008. Almost all results were negative in direction across prevalence, incidence, severity and self-report, and their conclusion is that formal juvenile justice processing appears to increase delinquency rather than reduce it. The pooled figures are weaker than that conclusion sounds. For the prevalence of reoffending at first follow-up the review gives d = -.109, with an interval from -.24 to .02 and p = .103, and says in terms that processing has no statistically significant crime control effect on that measure. The result at longest follow-up is significant, at d = -.15, with an interval from -.265 to -.035 and p = .01. The choice of control group matters as well: trials that set processing against a diversion programme gave much larger negative effects than trials that set it against doing nothing. Augustyn, Ward, Krohn and Dong followed 312 parent and child dyads in Rochester. They report that involuntary police contact between the ages of 14 and 16 predicted higher self-reported offending at 17, with the effect larger where the focal parent had an arrest history. They call this deviance amplification. Neither line of work tests the loop, and neither involves the press. Cohen's own verdict in his introduction to the third edition of 2002 was that the link between moral panics and folk devils is the book's weakest, and that the robust critiques of stimulus and response models had hardly touched what he called the thin idea of media-induced deviancy amplification.

limits: Wilkins's book was not read. Both Internet Archive copies are lending copies, and their full-text endpoints answered with a 401 on 21 September 2026, so his wording reaches this page through Cohen's citation of his chapter 4. The 311 pages given above come from the Internet Archive catalogue record rather than from the book. Young's Drugtakers and his 1971 chapter on the police as amplifiers were not obtained either, and are named here rather than quoted. Cohen's study is one case, worked up from documents and observation after the events, and it reports no measurement of deviance before and after the coverage. He says so himself. He contrasts the amplification model with disaster research, where the sequence has been empirically established, and writes that this is by no means the case for reactions to deviance. Petrosino and colleagues' review was read, but as the Japanese translation deposited at Kyoto University under the same title, authors and identifier, so the English wording of its results is not quoted here. Its pooled figures are given in prose rather than in this site's structured effect-size fields, because the headline prevalence result is not statistically significant. Lowry and colleagues' article was not obtained. Wiley and Oxford both answer with a Cloudflare challenge, no open copy is recorded, and the three figures given above come from the publisher's own abstract page. The Augustyn figures are associations in an observational cohort, not an experiment, and were read in the author manuscript at PubMed Central rather than in the published article. Cultivation and the fear-of-crime literature carry the media half of the argument, and this site covers that separately under mean world syndrome, entry no. 91.
misreadings: The model is not the claim that reporting violence makes people violent. It says that the reaction sorts people into a category, and that being sorted changes what they do next. The second error is treating amplification as automatic. Cohen calls the sequence typical rather than inevitable, and devotes space to de-amplification, in which constant harassment makes the identity unattractive and new recruits stay away. The third is reading moral panic and deviancy amplification as the same idea. One is a description of how a public reaction is organised, the other a causal claim about what that reaction does, and Cohen kept them apart while conceding the join between them was weak. The fourth concerns the famous numbers. The Daily Express and Daily Mirror headlines after Clacton reported 97 arrests, and 97 arrests is what happened. Cohen's charge was over-reporting of scale and menace, in phrases such as orgy of destruction and screaming mob, and in the generic plural that turned one overturned boat into boats. He did not argue that the events were invented. A £513 damage bill and a starting pistol are still a £513 damage bill and a starting pistol.

sources.text: Cohen, S. (2011). Folk Devils and Moral Panics: The Creation of the Mods and Rockers. Routledge Classics. First published 1972 by MacGibbon and Kee; third edition 2002. Read in full, but as the 1987 Basil Blackwell reprint of the 1972 text with Cohen's 1980 introduction, open at the Internet Archive. Every figure on this page comes from that text. The third edition reprints it and adds a new introduction, listed separately below.

Cohen, S. (2002). Introduction to the Third Edition: Moral Panics as Cultural Politics. In Folk Devils and Moral Panics, 3rd ed. London: Routledge. Read in full from a scan posted by the UK Data Service, and the source of the Young and McLuhan credit and of Cohen's weakest link verdict.

Wilkins, L. T. (1964). Social Deviance: Social Policy, Action and Research. London: Tavistock, 311 pages. Not read. Both Internet Archive copies are lending copies whose full-text endpoints answered 401 on 21 September 2026, and the page count comes from the catalogue record. Described on this page from Cohen's account of its chapter 4.

Young, J. (1971). The role of the police as amplifiers of deviancy, negotiators of reality and translators of fantasy: Some aspects of our present system of drug control as seen in Notting Hill. In S. Cohen (Ed.), Images of Deviance. Harmondsworth: Penguin. Not obtained. The Internet Archive copy of Images of Deviance is a lending copy that answered 401 on 21 September 2026. Cited here as Cohen cites it, from the first note to his third edition introduction.

Young, J. (1972). The Drugtakers: The Social Meaning of Drug Use. London: Paladin. Not obtained; the Internet Archive copy answered 403 on 21 September 2026. Cohen's own notes cite the book as The Drug Takers: The Social Meaning of Drug-Taking, Paladin, 1971, and the details here follow the Internet Archive record instead.

Lowry, D. T., Nio, T. C. J., & Leitner, D. W. (2003). Setting the public fear agenda: A longitudinal analysis of network TV crime reporting, public perceptions of crime, and FBI crime statistics. Journal of Communication, 53(1), 61-73. Full text not obtained: Wiley and Oxford both answer with a Cloudflare challenge, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex record no open copy. The three figures used here come from the abstract on the publisher's page, read through a Wayback Machine capture of 21 March 2022.

Petrosino, A., Turpin-Petrosino, C., & Guckenburg, S. (2010). Formal system processing of juveniles: Effects on delinquency. Campbell Systematic Reviews, 6(1), 1-88. Read for its results, but as the Japanese translation deposited in Kyoto University's KURENAI repository under the same identifier, fetched from the repository's REST bitstream route. Wiley and SAGE both answered 403 with a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026.

National Institute of Justice. Practice profile: Formal system processing for juveniles. CrimeSolutions. Read on 21 September 2026. It gives the prevalence result as d = -.109 across 27 studies and says the difference was not statistically significant.

Augustyn, M. B., Ward, J. T., Krohn, M. D., & Dong, B. (2019). Criminal justice contact across generations: Assessing the intergenerational labeling hypothesis. Journal of Developmental and Life-Course Criminology, 5(2), 137-175. Read in full as the author manuscript at PubMed Central, PMC6779300. The published article was not obtained, and the two versions were not compared.

McLaughlin, E. (2014). See also Young, 1971: Marshall McLuhan, moral panics and moral indignation. Theoretical Criminology, 18(4), 422-431. Read in full as the accepted manuscript at City Research Online. It traces the phrase to McLuhan as well, but cites the 1967 Sphere edition of Understanding Media at page 89, not the 1964 edition Cohen names.
